title: The Slide Designer Trap
author: Dr. Dario Emanuele
summary: Emanuele argues that the unspoken expectation for teachers to build lesson slides from scratch — functioning as unpaid digital content creators — is a core driver of teacher burnout. Drawing on his own training year experience of working until 2 AM to produce PowerPoint decks, he traces how this 'Slide Designer Trap' hijacks the time and cognitive energy teachers need to develop the foundational pedagogical competencies that actually define good teaching: behaviour management, live explanation, and adaptive response to students. The trap worsens over time because teachers develop an unhealthy dependency on static slide decks as a security blanket, which paradoxically sabotages responsive teaching — they cannot pivot when a student reveals a misconception because they are locked into a rigid digital script. Emanuele argues the systemic fix is centralised, fully-sequenced lesson banks so teachers can stop reinventing the wheel each evening and redirect their finite energy to the craft of teaching itself.
points: Novice teachers building slides from scratch spend so much time on digital design that they cannot develop the other Teachers' Standards — behaviour management, adaptive explanation, and curriculum knowledge — that actually determine teaching quality.

The 'Slide Designer Trap' creates a vicious cycle: no centralised resources forces slide creation, which causes exhaustion, which prevents mastery of pedagogy, which leads burnout — and veteran teachers face the same burden in mutated form each time they change schools.

Static, hyper-designed slides actively sabotage responsive teaching: a teacher locked into a rigid digital script cannot pivot when a student's answer reveals a deep misconception — the slide deck becomes a constraint rather than a tool.

Students do not care about slide transitions or custom colour palettes; they need a teacher who has the energy, clarity, and focus to teach them properly — which is impossible when planning consumes 16-hour days.

Centralised, fully-sequenced lesson banks are not a luxury but a necessity: they free teachers from the role of content creator and allow 100% of intellectual energy to go toward explaining, scaffolding, and responding to learners.
quotes: I want to take you back in time to 2015, the year I started my initial teacher training. I was placed in a fantastic school with brilliant colleagues, a supportive atmosphere, and an abundance of good intentions. Yet, it was during this exact year that my relationship with planning became toxic, setting off a cycle where I risked burning out more times than I care to admit.

All of a sudden, my days were entirely hijacked by digital design. This endless scramble to build PowerPoint decks took a massive toll. It stripped away the physical and mental time I desperately needed to develop and practise the other core competencies required of an educator.

I wasn't handed a single base slide to start from. Instead, I was pointed toward a chaotic shared drive, a digital graveyard of unorganised folders, random PDF files, and fragmented decks from years gone by. To survive the next morning, I found myself working until 2:00 AM, scouring the internet for worksheets, clipping images, and aligning text boxes.

The only reason I didn't join the statistics of those who quit during their training year was an intense, stubborn love for teaching and a deep pool of intrinsic motivation. I gritted my teeth, passed my training, and officially entered the profession.

I fell into the trap of believing that if my slides looked flawless and I followed them line by line, the lesson would be a success. It was a lie. Static, hyper-designed slides don't make a lesson successful; in fact, they actively sabotage your ability to deliver true responsive teaching.

Students do not care about your slide transitions, custom fonts, or colour palettes. They don't need a graphic designer. They are perfectly happy with a piece of paper, a visualiser, or a blank whiteboard, provided they are being taught by a teacher who has the energy, clarity, and focus to teach them properly.

Schools are accidentally sending a message to both new and veteran teachers that their primary value lies in their ability to curate digital assets, rather than their ability to deliver explicit instruction, scaffold learning, and manage a classroom.

The introduction of fully planned, high-quality, centralised lesson resources is not a luxury; it is an absolute necessity. When a school provides an established, evidence-based instructional framework as a baseline, teachers are instantly liberated.” Archived from Dr Dario Emanuele (Substack) on June 19, 2026 by Tim.
